newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire war hits railway that helped revive economy.
newsitem.headline: Zaire war hits railway that helped revive economy.

text.p: A railway has breathed life back into the south of Zaire just when the patient looked terminally ill, thanks to the return of some of the first big foreign investors after two decades of nationalisation.
Encroaching civil war is now hampering the Belgian-South African Sizarail consortium which came in 1995 to manage the state-owned railways and start trains running again.
But like other investors who have put their money on an economic revival in chronically mismanaged Zaire, Sizarail says it has no intention of running away.

"We are optimistic and we're here for the long term," said Patrick Claes, who leads 13 other Belgians in running Sizarail from Zaire's second city, Lubumbashi, the capital of the mineral-rich Shaba province along Zambia's border.
Sizarail reopened vital supply lines to southern Africa for an economy dependent on diamond and copper mines.

The appalling roads are too slow. Vehicles take several hours to cover 100 km and are often damaged on the way. Air links, which the diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi had to use before the railway reopened, are too expensive.
The six-month-old civil war has taken its toll as a relentless rebel march southwards and westwards cuts off line after line.
The biggest blow came this week when rebels took Kamina, cutting Sizarail's artery through which maize, coal and other imports reach Kasai province and its capital Mbuji-Mayi.
"If the railway is cut, economic life will dive, there will be a social drama," said Kasongo Tshikomba, deputy regional director of Zairean railways, SNCZ, which owns the lines.
"The railway allowed ordinary people to make some kind of a living, going to buy a bit of maize or fish and coming to sell it in the market. They can't travel any other way."
Lubumbashi always had road and rail access to its southern neighbour Zambia, just 30 km away, and from there to South Africa whose goods fill the city's trading stores.
Even maize is imported because transport to fertile agricultural land upcountry in Zaire was so bad. Maize grown there could rot in the fields while there were food shortages in cities.
It is these upcountry areas for whom Sizarail has transformed life.

Before the war started in October, it had knocked into shape lines linking Lubumbashi with Mwene Ditu, the nearest station to Mbuji-Mayi, and from there to Ilebo, a river port for boats to Kinshasa, several hundred kilometres away.
The railway, after years without investment, is still slow and the boat even slower.
The Lubumbashi-Kinshasa trip of more than 2,000 km can take a couple of weeks and southeast Zaire seems to have decided it's just not worth it.
"Hardly anything comes here any more from Kinshasa apart from a few bottles of beer and some cloth," said Claes.
"This area will become increasingly dependent economically on South Africa, and that's where the finances will come from."

Sizarail was also operating a line from Kamina to Kalemie, an inland port on Lake Tanganyika in east Zaire that fell to rebels in February. It was also slowly reviving the network around the jungle city of Kisangani that fell last month.
Zairean authorities forbid it to try to keep operating in rebel-held territory, so traffic and profits have plummeted.
"We have had a very bad start to this year," said Claes. "We have lost 50 percent of our traffic."
Shaba province is dominated by Gecamines, a state-owned mining giant that despite great potential has ground to a halt under mismanagement, official corruption and debt.
It had accounted for a third of Sizarail's traffic as it brought in coal, petrol and food for its workers.
Gecamines and its diamond-mine equivalent MIBA in next-door Kasai are major holders of the 49 percent Zairean interest in Sizarail, which employs 7,700 people.
Claes said that the consortium made $1 million profit in the year to June 30, 1996, the first full year of operation, on a turnover of $66 million. It invested $6 million over the same period.
